archetype.name: Pocket Passer (middle-of-field)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower who makes his money working the ball between the numbers at 10-plus air yards from the pocket. This year he has largely stopped using his legs, and the short and screen game around him adds little.

report.headline: The downfield leap is real; the September pace isn't, and the floor is shaky.
report.take:
Bryce Young in year four is a different passer on paper than the one who averaged 188 yards a game last season. He sits sixth in passing yards per game at 266.3, his yards per attempt are up 0.79, and his bad-throw rate has dropped from 15.3% to 12.7%. The shape of his game hasn't changed. Time to throw and aggressiveness are almost identical to 2025. He is still a smallish pocket thrower whose best work comes in rhythm over the middle. The difference is where the production comes from. On throws of 10+ air yards he is at +0.531 EPA per attempt with a +5.5 CPOE, and over the middle he is completing 73.4% with an +11.3 CPOE and no interceptions. That is a real skill showing up, and Tetairoa McMillan (0.285 EPA per target on 79 targets) gives it a destination.

The volume has context. Carolina passes more than situation predicts by 3 points (4th in the league), and its defense is 23rd in pass EPA with the league's worst sack rate. That keeps Young throwing all afternoon. Week 1 is the poster child: 361 yards in a 59-37 loss. He has been better trailing by 9+ (+0.085 EPA per play) than in one-score games (-0.024). His overall efficiency is only middle of the pack, 22nd in EPA per dropback and 29th in CPOE. The yardage rank flatters him.

What the season line hides is how front-loaded it is. Weeks 1, 2 and 4 produced +13.5, +10 and +16.6 passing EPA. Over his last five games he is at -0.099 EPA per dropback with a -5.7 CPOE and a 9.7% sack rate, and his whole season's positive EPA is essentially September's. Some of that is schedule: Tampa (2nd-ranked defense) and Green Bay (7th) were brutal, and against the Packers his intended air yards fell to 4.7. But he also went -5.8 EPA with a -9.9 CPOE against a 23rd-ranked New Orleans defense. The leaks are structural. Throws behind the line have cost 14.7 EPA. Third down sits at -0.256 EPA with 14 sacks and a 31.8% conversion rate. The left side of the field (-5.1 CPOE) is where his four interceptions live.

Where it heads: the downfield profile has held up across all nine starts often enough to trust. The scheme around it, with screens that don't work, third-and-long, and no designed or improvised running, caps the floor. Expect a passer who sits closer to his recent 225-230 yards a game than his 4,528-yard pace, with spike weeks when a defense lets him work the intermediate middle.

strengths.title: Intermediate and deep accuracy
strengths.body: Beyond 10 air yards he is completing throws well above expectation and generating the bulk of his value: +0.474 EPA on 10-19 yard throws and +0.639 on 20+. Those throws added +58.4 EPA in total, against a season total of 15.6. The 38 deep attempts are a small sample and will cool, but the CPOE on both bands is positive. That suggests placement, not just a few busted coverages.

strengths.title: Owns the middle of the field
strengths.body: Between the hashes he is at +0.514 EPA per attempt, a 60.8% success rate, an +11.3 CPOE and zero interceptions. That is where his anticipation and McMillan's work in traffic meet. It is the most repeatable part of his game because it rests on timing rather than arm talent, and it is what defenses have to take away.

strengths.title: Cleaner ball, sacks not his fault
strengths.body: His bad-throw rate dropped 2.6 points from last year to 12.7%, 11th among 42 charted passers. Under pressure he still converts only 25% of pressures into sacks, 14th best, in line with his 2024-25 form. The 7.9% sack rate comes from how often he is pressured (28.6%, 38th of 42), not from holding the ball.

concerns.title: Five-week efficiency slide
concerns.body: Since Week 6 he is at -0.099 EPA per dropback with a -5.7 CPOE, well off his season marks. Tampa and Green Bay explain part of it. A -9.9 CPOE game against the 23rd-ranked Saints defense does not. This is the real question for the rest of the year: whether September was the true level or a hot start against soft coverage.

concerns.title: Short game and screens bleed
concerns.body: Everything under 10 air yards is net negative (-0.014 EPA). Throws behind the line have lost 14.7 EPA with a -9.9 CPOE, so the easy-yardage part of the offense isn't easy. That is partly design and blocking rather than his accuracy. Still, it means drives that don't hit an intermediate shot often stall.

concerns.title: Third down and lost legs
concerns.body: Third down is a problem: -0.256 EPA, 14 sacks and a 31.8% conversion rate at 8.3 yards to go on average. The long distances are partly a product of the early-down screen game. He has also all but stopped running, down 8.2 rushing yards a game from 2025 after three seasons of 200-plus rushing yards. His eight scrambles have been productive (+0.49 EPA each), which makes the reluctance look like a choice that costs him an escape valve.

trend.note: Three big EPA games in the first four weeks, then negative passing EPA in four of the last five. Week 9 against Denver (+5.7, +11.1 CPOE) is the lone recent game that looked like September. The Week 10 win over New Orleans came despite him, not because of him.

nextGame.headline: A deep-leaky defense and its WR1 problem meet his best throws.
nextGame.body:
Baltimore's pass defense is only 21st in EPA, and its weaknesses line up with what Young does well. It is 27th against deep passes (+0.777 EPA) and has bled +0.72 EPA per target to opposing WR1s, 31st of 32, which points straight at McMillan. The catch is underneath: the Ravens are 6th against short throws (-0.069 EPA). That is where Carolina's screen game already struggles, so his day depends on whether the play-calling gets him to the intermediate middle instead of feeding the part of the field Baltimore shuts down. Baltimore also hits quarterbacks at the 10th-highest rate, a real issue for a passer already pressured as often as anyone. Carolina is a 2.5-point home favorite with a modest 43.5 total.

Availability tilts the script more than the matchup. Lamar Jackson is on IR with a thumb injury and is expected out 6-10 weeks, which should drag the Ravens offense down. That makes a pass-every-down shootout less likely and caps Young's volume ceiling, even as it improves Carolina's chances to play from ahead, where he has been efficient in a small sample. On Baltimore's defense, DT Nnamdi Madubuike (73% of snaps) left Monday's game with a hamstring and is questionable. Without him the interior pressure that hurts a 5-foot-10 passer would ease. Safety Jaylinn Hawkins (81% of snaps) was out Monday with a knee injury; if he stays out, the back end that already leaks deep gets thinner. Carolina's own report holds nothing that touches him: Brady Christensen hasn't played this year and Jonathon Brooks is a backup back.

keyMatchups.title: McMillan against a leaky WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: His top target has been his most productive receiver, and Baltimore has allowed WR1s to beat their usual output by 2.1 PPR points a game while giving up 0.72 EPA per target. The rank rests on a few games and on who the Ravens happened to face, but it fits a defense that is 27th on deep throws.

keyMatchups.title: Short game into strength
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore's best coverage area is short throws, and Young's under-10 work is already net negative. If Carolina leans on screens and checkdowns again, as it did at Green Bay, expect another sub-200-yard, negative-EPA line.

keyMatchups.title: Hits on a pressured passer
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore's hit rate ranks 10th while its sack rate is only 22nd, so it gets to quarterbacks without finishing. That suits Young's knack for avoiding sacks under pressure but threatens his accuracy. Madubuike's hamstring is the swing.

nextGame.watch: How often he throws between the numbers at 10+ air yards on early downs. That is where Baltimore is soft and where his season was built, versus another diet of screens into the Ravens' stingy short defense.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume should stay. Carolina passes more than situation predicts, and its defense, 23rd against the pass and last in sack rate, will keep putting him in catch-up mode. What won't hold is the September efficiency. His 4.7% TD rate and the deep-ball EPA rest on small samples, and his red-zone touchdowns (12) came on below-average red-zone efficiency. The improved ball placement and middle-of-field accuracy look real, and he hasn't been a turnover machine. Expect more weeks like his recent ones than his first month, with occasional spikes against secondaries that let him work the intermediate middle.

I'd project 225-260 passing yards a game and 1.2-1.7 touchdowns. Sacks should keep landing around 3 to 4 a game unless protection improves, because the pressure volume, not his decision-making, is the driver. Rushing stays near zero unless he rediscovers the scrambles that paid off earlier in his career, which leaves his fantasy floor thinner than a typical 260-yard passer's.
swingFactors: Play-calling share of intermediate middle throws vs screens

confidence.note: Nine starts with a stable role and target tree, but efficiency has swung hard between a hot first month and a cold five-game stretch.
